title: John McCarthy and the Creation of Lisp (1958)
explainer: John McCarthy designed Lisp in 1958 at MIT because FORTRAN, the only high-level language then available, had no support for recursion or conditional expressions, the tools he needed for his AI research. The result was a language built around functions as the primary unit of computation, including functions that take and return other functions. Nearly every idea this lesson covers, from first-class functions to recursion as a default, traces back to choices McCarthy made to solve a specific research problem, not to an abstract theory of programming handed down in advance.

title: Currying: Schönfinkel's Logic Trick Renamed After Curry
explainer: The idea that a multi-argument function can be rewritten as a chain of one-argument functions was first worked out by Moses Schönfinkel in a 1920 talk at Göttingen, as a way to simplify combinatory logic; Haskell Curry independently expanded the technique later, and later writers attached Curry's name to it rather than Schönfinkel's. Every time you partially apply a function in a functional language, you're using a maneuver invented decades before compilers existed, to make formal logic simpler. It's a reminder that much of functional programming's toolkit is repurposed 1920s mathematical logic, not a recent invention.
